scenes.narration: Nvidia designs the most sought-after AI processor on the planet.
Tech giants wire tens of billions of dollars just to reserve future racks.
Yet inside brand-new data centers, rows of thirty-thousand-dollar servers sit waiting.
Not because Nvidia forgot how to design silicon.
They are waiting on tiny stacked memory cubes sitting millimeter-close beside the processor.
Those cubes are called High Bandwidth Memory, or HBM.
And over half of the world's AI supply comes from one South Korean underdog: SK Hynix.
Here is why that makes no sense on paper.
For three decades, Samsung dominated global memory like an untouchable empire.
Samsung had bigger fabs, deeper cash reserves, and even helped draft early HBM standards.
Then, in 2019, Samsung looked at HBM's tiny sales and disbanded its core development team.
Executives bet the future belonged to standard server and smartphone memory instead.
Meanwhile, rival SK Hynix kept funding a weird vertical chip it first built in 2013.
For nearly ten years, that bet looked like an expensive commercial dead end.
Gamers didn't want to pay extra for exotic stacked silicon.
Then ChatGPT arrived, and overnight every AI lab hit the exact same physical wall.
Nvidia locked up SK Hynix's entire HBM calendar a full year before chips even left the fab.
When Samsung rushed back in, its twelve-layer stacks ran into brutal heat and yield traps.
Even wilder, every gigabyte of HBM devours roughly three times the wafer space of normal RAM.
So feeding AI servers started starving laptops, phones, and cloud memory worldwide.
One forgotten gaming experiment quietly became the tollbooth of artificial intelligence.
Why can't the fastest GPU on earth think without stacked memory right beside it?
How did liquid glue give SK Hynix a multi-year manufacturing lead over Samsung?
And why does SK Hynix's biggest victory now force a dangerous new dependency on TSMC?
To understand how SK Hynix cornered AI, we have to go back to a desperate GPU gamble in 2013.
